analysis.one_liner: Guarantees people with disabilities the right to receive long-term care at home instead of in institutions.
analysis.headline: A bill making it illegal to force people with disabilities into nursing homes to get care won the support of 224 House members — a majority — but never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it discrimination for states and long-term care insurers to deny people with disabilities home and community-based care when they qualify for a nursing home or other institution. It bans waiting lists and cost caps that block home care, requires states to plan and pay for moving people out of institutions (with up to 12 years to comply), and lets individuals sue — with the Justice Department also enforcing, backed by fines up to $100,000 for a first violation.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need help with daily living and qualify for institutional placement — including seniors, people with intellectual or developmental disabilities, and people with physical disabilities — along with their families and unpaid caregivers. The bill would give them a federally enforceable right to receive that care in their own homes and communities, with maximum control over who provides it, instead of being placed in a nursing facility to get the same care. It also requires states to address the shortage of accessible, affordable housing and to pay home care workers rates sufficient to sustain the workforce.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with disabilities needing long-term care and families

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal discrimination for a state or long-term care insurer to deny, delay, or cap community-based services for anyone who qualifies for an institutional placement, so care can no longer come with a requirement to enter a nursing home.
Specifically bans waiting lists, service and cost caps, and policies that force people to rely on informal family caregivers or receive services in congregate, disability-specific settings.

Requires every state to file a transition plan with measurable annual targets for moving people out of institutions and shifting funding to home and community-based care, with full compliance required within 12 years.

Gives individuals the right to sue in federal court — with possible appointment of an attorney, no filing fees, punitive damages, and emergency orders to prevent institutionalization — while the Attorney General must investigate violations and can seek civil penalties of up to $100,000 for a first violation and $200,000 thereafter.

Requires states to establish payment rates high enough to sustain a home care workforce, and to ensure an adequate supply of affordable, accessible, integrated housing so people have a real choice of where to live.

analysis.who_pays: State and local Medicaid programs, which fund most long-term care, would bear the cost of guaranteeing home and community-based services to everyone who qualifies for institutional care — the bill appropriates no federal money for this. Private long-term care insurers would face the same coverage mandates. Nursing homes, long-term care hospitals, and psychiatric institutions would lose residents and revenue as people gain an enforceable right to be served at home.
analysis.who_pays_short: State Medicaid programs, insurers, and nursing homes

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates no federal money, so states would have to finance a major expansion of home and community-based care largely from their own Medicaid budgets — a substantial unfunded mandate, and one that could crowd out other state priorities.
States would have up to 12 years after enactment to fully comply, meaning people currently in institutions could wait many years, if not decades, before the right becomes real for them.

The main enforcement tool is litigation — individuals can seek punitive damages and courts can levy fines — so change could come through lawsuits against state agencies rather than through funded, cooperative expansion of services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people affected, the benefit is hard to overstate: today, in most states the only reliable way to get long-term care through Medicaid is to move into a nursing home, and this bill would make that choice illegal discrimination. The costs are also real — no new federal funding is attached, so the burden falls on state Medicaid budgets, and the 12-year compliance window means relief would arrive slowly even for those who need it now. A stronger bill would have paired the mandate with federal money; as written, it relies on states, insurers, and lawsuits to deliver the promise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired automatically when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on April 19, 2023, with 60 original cosponsors, and it was referred to both the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees.
Support grew to 224 cosponsors — more than a majority of the House, including 16 Republicans — yet the bill never advanced past referral.
The action history shows only two entries for the bill's entire two-year life: introduction and committee referral. No hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, all unpassed bills died, and the bill would have had to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing homes and other institutional care providers keep their residents and Medicaid revenue, and states avoid a large new spending mandate. The people the bill was written for — those in or facing institutional placement — and the family members who care for them gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Institutional care providers and state budgets

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 60 original cosponsors across both parties on day one.

for.name: 224 House cosponsors
for.role: A majority of the House, including 208 Democrats and 16 Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill more support than needed to pass the chamber — support that was never tested with a vote.

for.name: Disability rights advocates and self-advocacy groups
for.what_they_did: Championed the legislation, which is named for Latonya Reeves, a disability rights activist who fought to leave an institution, and pressed Congress for a federal right to home and community-based care.

against.name: Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but the committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill at any point in the two-year Congress.

against.name: Chair Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but the committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill at any point in the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never allowed floor time for a bill that a majority of the chamber had signed onto, leaving it to die in committee without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 208 of 224 — with only 16 of the chamber's 222 Republicans signing on; because the bill never reached a committee or floor vote, no actual vote record exists.

industries.industry: Nursing facilities and other institutional care providers
industries.note: The bill defines nursing homes, long-term care hospitals, psychiatric institutions, and isolating congregate settings as 'institutions' and gives their residents an enforceable right to be served at home instead. These providers' revenue depends on Medicaid-funded institutional placements, so every person who transitions out is a lost bed.

industries.industry: Home and community-based care agencies and home care workers
industries.note: The bill requires states to set payment rates sufficient to sustain a workforce that can support people living at home, expanding demand for in-home aides and community services. Its interest in the bill runs alongside the public's: more people served at home means more work, not higher charges for the same care.

The bill applies its nondiscrimination mandate to any public or private entity that funds long-term services and supports, requiring them to pay for community-based care rather than limiting or capping it. That expands their coverage obligations.
